steps.title: Stopping distance is two distances
steps.body:
A car does not stop the moment the driver sees a hazard. First the driver has to react, and the car keeps going at full speed: the **thinking distance**. Then the brakes act and the car slows to a stop: the **braking distance**.

$$\text{stopping distance} = \text{thinking distance} + \text{braking distance}$$

The Highway Code gives typical figures. At 30 mph (about 13 m/s) the thinking distance is 9 m and the braking distance 14 m, so the stopping distance is 23 m. At 70 mph it is 96 m, about the length of a football pitch. Notice that the thinking distance grows in proportion to speed, but the braking distance grows much faster.

visuals.alt: A table of Highway Code typical stopping distances at 20 to 70 mph: thinking distance rising from 6 m to 21 m, braking distance from 6 m to 75 m, and total from 12 m to 96 m

check.prompt: A driver's thinking distance is 12 m and the braking distance is 24 m. What is the stopping distance?

steps.title: Thinking distance: speed times reaction time
steps.body:
During the driver's **reaction time** the car travels at its full speed, so:

$$\text{thinking distance} = \text{speed} \times \text{reaction time}$$

This is just $s = v t$. A typical reaction time is between **0.2 s and 0.9 s**. At 15 m/s with a reaction time of 0.7 s, the thinking distance is $15 \times 0.7 = 10.5$ m.

Double the speed and the thinking distance doubles. Anything that slows the driver's reactions makes it longer: tiredness, alcohol, drugs, and distractions such as a phone.

visuals.alt: A card showing thinking distance equals speed times reaction time, with units m, m/s and s

check.prompt: A car travels at 15 m/s. The driver's reaction time is 0.7 s. Calculate the thinking distance.

steps.title: Measuring reaction time
steps.body:
Reaction time can be measured with a computer test, clicking when the screen changes, or with the **ruler drop test**: a partner holds a ruler between your open finger and thumb, drops it without warning, and you catch it. The further it falls before you catch it, the slower your reaction.

The distance is converted to a time using $s = \tfrac{1}{2} g t^2$, or a conversion table. Repeat several times and take a mean, because reaction time varies. The test is only fair if the person catching cannot see when the ruler will be released.

The factors that lengthen reaction time are the ones that appear in the exam: tiredness, alcohol, drugs and distractions.

check.solution: Alcohol slows the driver's reactions, lengthening the thinking distance. The other three affect how quickly the car can slow down, which is braking distance.

steps.title: From ruler drop to reaction time
steps.body: A dropped ruler is in free fall, so the distance it falls in time $t$ is $s = \tfrac{1}{2} g t^2$. Rearranging gives $t = \sqrt{2 s / g}$. Keep the distance in metres.

steps.text: Repeat and take a mean; a single catch is not reliable

steps.title: What lengthens the braking distance
steps.body:
Braking distance depends on how quickly the brakes can take kinetic energy out of the car, and on how much there is to take.

- **Road conditions**: wet or icy roads reduce the friction between tyres and road, so the tyres can grip less and the car takes longer to slow.
- **Vehicle condition**: worn tyres grip less; worn brakes produce less friction.
- **Speed**: the faster the car, the more kinetic energy it has, and doubling the speed gives *four times* the kinetic energy.

A heavier car, such as a loaded lorry, also has more kinetic energy at the same speed.

check.prompt: Why does an icy road increase the braking distance?
check.solution: Less friction between tyres and road means a smaller braking force, so the car takes longer, and further, to stop.
options: Ice reduces the friction between the tyres and the road
Ice increases the driver's reaction time
Ice makes the brakes wear out faster

steps.title: What braking does to the energy
steps.body:
When the brakes are applied, friction between the brake pads and the wheels does **work** on the car. That work transfers energy from the car's **kinetic energy** store to the **thermal energy** store of the brakes, so their temperature rises.

To stop in a given distance, the work done by the brakes must equal the kinetic energy: $F s = \tfrac{1}{2} m v^2$. A greater speed means more kinetic energy, so a greater braking force is needed to stop in the same distance.

A very large braking force gives a very large **deceleration**. That can make the brakes overheat and lose effectiveness, and can cause the car to skid, so the driver loses control.

check.prompt: Which statement about braking is correct?
check.solution: Work done by friction transfers the car's kinetic energy to the thermal store of the brakes, which get hotter. Energy is transferred, never destroyed.
options: Kinetic energy is destroyed by the brakes
Friction transfers energy from the kinetic store to the thermal store of the brakes
The brakes convert thermal energy into kinetic energy
The car's kinetic energy is stored in the brakes until it moves again

steps.title: Calculating a braking force
steps.body: Two routes give the same braking force. The energy route: kinetic energy equals the work done by the brakes. The motion route: $v^2 - u^2 = 2 a s$ gives the deceleration, then $F = m a$. Either scores; show the steps.

visuals.problem: A 1000 kg car travelling at 20 m/s stops in 40 m. Find the braking force.

steps.note: all of it has to go

steps.text: Work done by brakes $= F s = F \times 40$, so $F = 200\,000 \div 40 = 5000$ N

check.prompt: An 800 kg car travelling at 15 m/s stops in 30 m. Calculate the braking force.

steps.title: Double the speed, four times the braking distance
steps.body:
Braking distance is proportional to the **square** of the speed. From $F s = \tfrac{1}{2} m v^2$ with a fixed braking force, $s = m v^2 / 2F$, so $s \propto v^2$.

The graph shows braking distance against speed for a car that decelerates at 6.25 m/s²: 8 m at 10 m/s, 32 m at 20 m/s, 72 m at 30 m/s. Doubling the speed quadruples the braking distance; tripling it gives nine times.

The thinking distance, by contrast, is a straight line: it only doubles when the speed doubles. That is why the Highway Code's stopping distances grow so steeply.

visuals.alt: A graph of distance against speed with a curve for braking distance rising steeply through 8 m at 10 m/s, 32 m at 20 m/s and 72 m at 30 m/s, and a dashed straight line for thinking distance

check.prompt: A car's braking distance at 10 m/s is 8 m. What is its braking distance at 20 m/s, with the same braking force?
check.solution: Double the speed means four times the braking distance: $8 \times 4 = 32$ m.

steps.title: Your turn: kinetic energy the brakes must remove
steps.body:
Drag the speed of a 1000 kg car. The graph is $E_k = \tfrac{1}{2} m v^2$: the energy the brakes must transfer away to stop it. It is a curve, not a line, because of the square.

At 10 m/s the brakes remove 50 000 J; at 20 m/s, 200 000 J; at 30 m/s, 450 000 J. With the same braking force, the distance needed grows in exactly the same proportion.

visuals.fallback: A curve rising ever more steeply: 50 000 J at 10 m/s, 200 000 J at 20 m/s and 450 000 J at 30 m/s for a 1000 kg car.

check.prompt: How much kinetic energy does a 1000 kg car have at 20 m/s?

steps.title: Going deeper: estimating the forces in an emergency stop
steps.body:
Higher tier asks you to **estimate** the forces when a vehicle decelerates, and to say why large decelerations are dangerous. Work from speed and time to acceleration, then $F = m a$.

A 1200 kg car doing an emergency stop from 30 m/s in 3 s decelerates at $30 \div 3 = 10$ m/s², so the braking force is about $1200 \times 10 = 12\,000$ N, roughly the car's own weight. In a crash the same change of speed might happen in 0.1 s, giving 30 times the force.

A large deceleration is dangerous because the large force can make the tyres skid, so the driver loses control, and because the brakes can overheat and fade. Inside the car, the people decelerate too, and the force on them is what seat belts and air bags spread out over a longer time.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- Stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance.
- Thinking distance = speed × reaction time. Reaction time is typically 0.2 to 0.9 s and is lengthened by tiredness, alcohol, drugs and distractions.
- Braking distance is lengthened by wet or icy roads, worn tyres or brakes, and speed. It is proportional to speed squared: double the speed, four times the distance.
- Braking: friction does work, transferring kinetic energy to the thermal store of the brakes. $F s = \tfrac{1}{2} m v^2$.
- Large decelerations mean large forces: skidding, loss of control, overheating brakes. Estimate them with $a = \Delta v / t$ then $F = m a$.

Which factor increases the thinking distance?

questions.prompt: A 900 kg car travelling at 10 m/s stops in a braking distance of 15 m. Calculate the braking force.
questions.solution: $E_k = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 900 \times 10^2 = 45\,000$ J. Work done by the brakes equals this: $F = 45\,000 \div 15 = 3000$ N.

questions.prompt: A car's braking distance at 10 m/s is 8 m. Estimate its braking distance at 30 m/s with the same braking force.
questions.solution: Braking distance is proportional to speed squared. Three times the speed gives $3^2 = 9$ times the distance: $8 \times 9 = 72$ m.

questions.prompt: In the ruler drop test, what is actually measured?
questions.solution: The distance fallen is read off the ruler and converted to a time using $s = \tfrac{1}{2} g t^2$ or a table.

questions.prompt: Estimate the average braking force on a 1200 kg car that stops from 30 m/s in 3 s.
A driver has had very little sleep and is driving on a wet road. Explain why the car's stopping distance will be greater than normal. Refer to both parts of the stopping distance.
questions.solution: Stopping distance is thinking distance plus braking distance, and both are increased here. Tiredness increases the driver's reaction time, and thinking distance is speed multiplied by reaction time, so the car travels further at full speed before the brakes are even applied. The wet road reduces the friction between the tyres and the road surface, so the braking force is smaller. A smaller force does less work per metre, so more distance is needed to transfer all the car's kinetic energy to the thermal store of the brakes, and the braking distance increases. Both parts are longer, so the total is longer.

thinking distance = speed × reaction time, so it increases
wet road reduces friction between tyres and road
smaller braking force, so greater distance to remove the kinetic energy
clear conclusion linking both increases to a longer stopping distance

criteria.text: Identifies stopping distance as thinking distance plus braking distance
Thinking distance = speed × reaction time, so it increases
A wet road reduces friction between the tyres and the road
The braking force is smaller, so a greater distance is needed to do the work of removing the kinetic energy; braking distance increases
Concludes that both parts increase, so the stopping distance is greater

questions.modelAnswer: Stopping distance is the sum of the thinking distance and the braking distance, and in this situation both are longer than normal. The tired driver has a longer reaction time. During the reaction time the car travels at its full speed, and thinking distance equals speed multiplied by reaction time, so the thinking distance increases. The wet road reduces the friction between the tyres and the road surface. The braking force that friction can provide is therefore smaller. To stop, the brakes must do work equal to the car's kinetic energy, and work is force multiplied by distance, so a smaller force needs a greater distance: the braking distance increases. Because both the thinking distance and the braking distance are greater, the stopping distance is greater, and the driver should slow down to compensate.

questions.prompt: A car brakes with a constant braking force. Show that doubling the car's speed makes its braking distance four times as long.
questions.skill: show-that with kinetic energy and work done
questions.solution: The brakes must do work equal to the kinetic energy: $F s = \tfrac{1}{2} m v^2$, so $s = m v^2 / 2F$. With $m$ and $F$ constant, $s \propto v^2$. Doubling $v$ gives $(2v)^2 = 4 v^2$, so the braking distance is $4$ times as long.

markScheme.description: work done by brakes equals kinetic energy: $F s = \tfrac{1}{2} m v^2$
$s = m v^2 / 2F$, so $s \propto v^2$ with $F$ and $m$ constant
braking distance four times as long, stated

criteria.text: States that the work done by the brakes equals the kinetic energy: $F s = \tfrac{1}{2} m v^2$
Rearranges to show $s$ is proportional to $v^2$ when $F$ and $m$ are constant
Concludes the braking distance is four times as long

questions.modelAnswer: To stop the car, the brakes must transfer all of its kinetic energy by doing work. So $F s = \tfrac{1}{2} m v^2$, where $F$ is the braking force and $s$ the braking distance. Rearranging, $s = \dfrac{m v^2}{2F}$. The mass and the braking force are constant, so $s$ is proportional to $v^2$. If the speed doubles from $v$ to $2v$, then $v^2$ becomes $(2v)^2 = 4v^2$, four times as large. So the braking distance is four times as long, as required.

questions.prompt: A car travels at 25 m/s. The driver's reaction time is 0.6 s and the brakes give a deceleration of 6.25 m/s². Calculate the total stopping distance.
questions.solution: Thinking distance $= 25 \times 0.6 = 15$ m. Braking distance from $v^2 - u^2 = 2 a s$: $0 - 625 = 2 \times (-6.25) \times s$, so $s = 625 \div 12.5 = 50$ m. Stopping distance $= 15 + 50 = 65$ m.

questions.prompt: In a ruler drop test a student catches the ruler after it has fallen 30 cm. Use $s = \tfrac{1}{2} g t^2$ with $g = 9.8$ m/s² to calculate the reaction time. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
questions.skill: reaction time from a ruler drop
questions.solution: $t = \sqrt{2 s \div g} = \sqrt{2 \times 0.30 \div 9.8} = \sqrt{0.0612} = 0.247$ s, so **0.25 s**. Note the conversion of 30 cm to 0.30 m.

questions.prompt: A student says: *at 60 mph a car needs twice the stopping distance it needs at 30 mph, because it is going twice as fast.* Use the Highway Code figures (30 mph: thinking 9 m, braking 14 m; 60 mph: thinking 18 m, braking 55 m) to evaluate this statement.
questions.skill: evaluating a claim about stopping distances
questions.solution: At 30 mph the stopping distance is $9 + 14 = 23$ m. At 60 mph it is $18 + 55 = 73$ m. That is more than three times as far, not twice. The thinking distance does double, from 9 m to 18 m, because it is proportional to speed. But the braking distance goes from 14 m to 55 m, roughly four times, because it is proportional to speed squared. The student is right about the thinking distance and wrong about the total.

markScheme.description: thinking distance does double, because it is proportional to speed
braking distance roughly quadruples, because it is proportional to speed squared
conclusion: more than three times the distance, so the claim is wrong

criteria.text: The thinking distance does double, as it is proportional to speed
The braking distance is about four times, as it is proportional to speed squared
Concludes the total is more than three times, so the student's claim is wrong

questions.modelAnswer: At 30 mph the stopping distance is $9 + 14 = 23$ m. At 60 mph it is $18 + 55 = 73$ m, which is more than three times as far, so the student's claim is wrong. The student is partly right: the thinking distance does double, from 9 m to 18 m, because thinking distance is speed multiplied by reaction time and is proportional to speed. But the braking distance rises from 14 m to 55 m, almost four times, because the kinetic energy the brakes must remove is proportional to the square of the speed. Adding a doubled thinking distance to a quadrupled braking distance gives a total that is far more than double.

questions.prompt: In a crash, a 1500 kg car travelling at 20 m/s is brought to rest in 0.5 s. Estimate the average force on the car.
questions.solution: $a = 20 \div 0.5 = 40$ m/s². $F = m a = 1500 \times 40 = 60\,000$ N. A force this size is why crashes are so damaging; crumple zones lengthen the time and lower it.

questions.prompt: Put the events of an emergency stop in order.
questions.solution: Seeing, then the thinking distance at full speed, then braking with friction doing the work, then rest.
items: The driver's reaction time passes while the car continues at full speed
The driver presses the brake pedal, and friction between the pads and the wheels does work that transfers the car's kinetic energy to the thermal store of the brakes

questions.prompt: A 1000 kg car travelling at 20 m/s brakes to a stop. All of its kinetic energy is transferred to the thermal store of its four brake discs, which have a total mass of 10 kg and a specific heat capacity of 450 J/kg°C. Calculate the temperature rise of the discs. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
questions.skill: linking braking to specific heat capacity

examTechnique.body:
Stopping distance questions are half explanation and half calculation, and both halves want the split into thinking and braking made explicit. Name which distance a factor changes and give the mechanism: *reaction time* for the driver's factors, *friction between tyres and road* or *kinetic energy* for the car's.

The calculations are borrowed from earlier topics: $s = v t$ for thinking distance, then either $v^2 - u^2 = 2 a s$ or $F s = \tfrac{1}{2} m v^2$ for braking. State which you are using. When asked to *estimate* a force, use $a = \Delta v / t$ then $F = m a$, and comment on why a large deceleration is dangerous if the question invites it.
examinerErrors: Saying alcohol or tiredness affects the braking distance. They affect the driver, so the thinking distance.
Saying an icy road affects the thinking distance. It reduces friction, so the braking distance.
Claiming braking distance doubles when speed doubles. It quadruples, because kinetic energy depends on speed squared.
Writing that kinetic energy is *lost* or *used up*. It is transferred to the thermal store of the brakes by the work done by friction.
Leaving the ruler drop distance in centimetres inside $s = \tfrac{1}{2} g t^2$.
Estimating a braking force with the car's speed rather than its deceleration in $F = m a$.
Giving the danger of a large deceleration as *the car stops too quickly* rather than the large force causing skidding, loss of control or brake failure.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer separates the two distances every time, attaches each factor to the right one with its mechanism, and turns a Highway Code table into the two proportionalities: thinking distance with speed, braking distance with speed squared. It can show the square law from $F s = \tfrac{1}{2} m v^2$, convert a ruler drop to a reaction time with units handled, and estimate a deceleration force from typical values. It explains the danger of a large deceleration in terms of force, and links the energy transferred to a temperature rise of the brakes when asked.
